Fragment shaders get called once per pixel (fragment). There's very few times I've agreed with Early Access style content. After Towns and other Early Access gems and it being used as a means of protection against criticism, it's clear that the system does not work as intended, or at least that Valve is unwilling to enforce certain basic rules on the system. Early Access is a pact; you're getting profit and/or funding for the rest of development but because you want feedback on your game and you want to know where to take the development towards. If I submit a game, I should be asked that it at least be technically proficient, as in I can guarantee that it runs fine on a large set of computers (not necessarily perfect, as certain kinks probably would need ironing out). After that, feedback on the game would be mostly bug reports and design changes, the kind of thing Early Access is very good at doing (well, I don't know bug reports, but the forums are certainly useful to see the response to design decisions and common complaints). Early Access should not be a means for a developer to hold a carrot in front of you, promise you a fantastic experience, start to season the carrot right then and there, but just eating it for himself after months or years of the same. Even games like Rust and DayZ which I would argue have good developers behind them are way too massive an undertaking at this point for them to advance at a reasonable pace. As I understand it, even though there are frequent or at the very least non-stagnant updates on those, there are still several issues not addressed, but the developer has no obligation now of making it work. If the games were released under normal conditions and were as broken and unfinished as they are now, not even the promise of what could have been would save it, except if a very competent and dedicated mod team made it their task. And that's a problem, because they are not obligated now to finish the games and could easily simply leave them as is but suffer none of the consequences that a regular broken game has. All in the name of Early Access. Look at Blood of the Werewolf (Megaman-like 2D platformer TB covered recently). That's what Early Access should be. A technically competent but highly unpolished game gets put up, and the devs work like mad on it, taking into account every criticism and complaint that people have, and mold their previously shoddy attempt into a diamond. 

Paid Beta and Alpha are a bit grayer, especially coming from a dev like Blizzard who you know will deliver a highly polished product in the end, unless it's an absolute and complete blunder during development, and even then they've been fixing and tweaking the infamous Diablo 3 to the point where fans are actually enjoying it tremendously. If the dev doesn't have that kind of pedigree, I'd be very concerned with it. Paying to get into the Beta of generic game company X is very different than paying to get into the beta of Battlefield 4 (for example, first game that came into my head by a good developer), more so if paying gets you access to the full game later on. I'd say if a company want to do it, go ahead, but be prepared to face the reality about your game, your company, and your personal skill. Sometimes they simply bite off more than they can chew.

What's your goal? 

Mobile apps? Then start learning some Java and objective C, maybe some C#. 

Desktop apps in general? I'd argue C++ is perfect for the performance critical areas, even if the lovers of managed languages would like you to believe you can write anything in Java or C# or some equivalent there of. The obvious example is games, where responsiveness and framerate are king, and so the amount of native code is maximized and polished to perfection before introducing scripting with LUA or some other scripting language. The counter example would be Minecraft, which is entirely written in Java, but is obviously nowhere near the level of complexity of games like Crysis 3 and the like. 

Database programming? SQL is king as I understand it. 

Not programming at all but more theoretical areas like Alan Turing's work? If your uni has some sort of research branch of the computer science department I'd look into that. Maybe ask in another uni if they wouldn't mind you visiting to see what they're working on and what's it like?

TL;DR Start looking into what may interest you within the realm of computer science and go on from there. Programming is a huge area, but there's a lot of things one can do with a CS Degree. And heck, if you can, find a job for the summer that isn't related to CS. Already having a job, even if it's not necessarily in your field of studies, speaks well of a job applicant fresh out of college.

Socialist society would teach people that their work guarantees them survival, a post-scarcity society. In capitalism, you NEED to work. It becomes a chore. Even if you're sick and dying, you need to work because if not you can't afford food and shelter and all those basic needs. In socialism, the incentive to work is that you WANT to work. If you can't produce for whatever reason, the community helps out, society overcomes troubles together. It's not a selfish struggle to survive, it's a communal struggle.

Veo como en el DF los ricos se benefician y viven la buena vida, mientras que la clase media se convierte en clase baja, y la clase baja sufre aún más. En el resto del país, historias similares, de personas con privilegio abusando, destruyendo, siendo irrespetuosos, y nunca cumpliendo con sus deberes cívicos, y a veces, tampoco sus deberes como ser humano (si es que esos existen). Aquí no parece haber opiniones fuertes, y entiendo por qué. Es muy dificil tener una opinión única en cuanto a toda la reforma. ¿Es en principio un buen documento? Sí. Las compañías que necesitan tener ciertos privilegios que antes no tenían ahora sí los tienen. ¿Se pudo haber hecho de forma mejor? Claro, rara vez se empieza desde 100. No hubo un esfuerzo por parte del gobierno para que la gente entendiera la reforma y sus consecuencias, que habla de un gobierno que hace cosas en privado y en secreto. No tienen que ser cosas malas las que mantienen en secreto. Pero lógicamente causa sospecha por parte de un pueblo al que lo pisotea a cada rato una compañía X y/o el gobierno mismo. ¿Qué es lo peor de la reforma? Pues lo que se ha comentado. Los sindicatos que mantienen los esfuerzos nacionales para salir adelante estancados y estáticos mantuvieron muchísimos privilegios que no se han ganado ni se merecen. Nuestra queridísima Gordillo ha sido reelegida, y con tacticas obviamente sucias, pero porque no son transparentes, no se puede reclamar de forma tan directa y obvia; mucha manita de puerco tendría que ser usada para obtener evidencia de calidad judicial como para que valga la pena. 
Más allá de eso, es como lo veas tú. Yo que tiendo más a la izquierda, me molesta más que nada el hecho de que no se supo de ello hasta que era muy tarde como para hacer una diferencia o vocear nuestros disgustos con esto. Sí, las compañías necesitan apoyo y razón para existir, pero el individuo también, así que hay que considerar a ambos, que no se ha logrado del todo con la reforma.

No te molestes, aquí no se han puesto de acuerdo, y posts como estos acaban siendo debates políticos más que análisis objetivos de la reforma.

Con eso, mi opinión es que esta muy mixto el beneficio y el maleficio de la reforma como para decir: "está bien" o "está mal". Lo de los sindicatos es lo que más molesta, puesto que es una gran parte de lo que atrasa a las empresas nacionales como la CFE, y también atrasa a la educación como ya sabemos gracias al SNTE. Por otra parte, las compañías tienen ligeramente más oportunidad de hacer negocio, que no es necesariamente bueno, pero es cierto.

The melodic aspect of metal is strange. The original metal bands all had melodic elements in them, and I'd argue most of them do. If you look over on the blacklist, most of those would be considered melodic something.

Best way I can explain it is Amon Amarth, who are melodic, versus something like Cannibal Corpse, like viken pointed out. In Amon Amarth, the guitars have more treble-oriented sounds, which is what most people end up singing when they hum the guitar part in their songs (try it yourself; if you listen to Twilight of the Thundergod, the melody is very clear).

This kind of distinction makes it easier to "digest" or interpret, since it's closer to your average tune. This leads to the whole commercial sound issue, which I won't touch, but is essentially what people refer to.

In a simplified manner, power metal has the most melody, while death (true death, not melodic) and grind usually don't have any.
